tagline: From runes to Beowulf — a three-stage diploma in reading the language of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.
philosophy: Old English is not modern English with strange spellings. It is a fully inflected Germanic tongue with four cases, three genders, strong and weak nouns, and a verbal system closer to modern German than to Shakespeare. We teach it as a language to be read with notes, not spoken or composed. You will earn the right to sit down with Beowulf, Caedmon's Hymn, The Wanderer, and Bede — to read them in the original with a glossary and a grammar at your side. That is the goal. That is enough.
duration_estimate: 4–8 months at one hour per day
method: Reading-led. Grammar introduced in context. Every lesson contains a line or two of authentic Old English from the corpus. By the end of Stage 3 you will have read the opening of Beowulf and the whole of Caedmon's Hymn.
prerequisites: None. A knowledge of modern English grammar (what a noun is, what a verb is, what a case is) helps but is not required. We will teach the grammar as we go.

stages.name: The Sound and the Shape
stages.subtitle: The alphabet, the four extra letters, the long marks; reading aloud before parsing.
learning_outcomes: Read aloud any printed Old English text with accurate reconstructed pronunciation (West Saxon, c. 900–1000 CE).
Recognize and produce the four letters not found in modern English: æ (ash), þ (thorn), ð (eth), ƿ (wynn).
Distinguish long and short vowels and mark them with macrons where traditional editions do.
Pronounce the consonant clusters (sc = sh, cg = dge) and the guttural h and g that have no modern English equivalents.

lessons.title: The Alphabet
lessons.content: Twenty-four letters borrowed from Latin plus four Germanic holdovers. The long s (ſ) sometimes appears in manuscripts; the modern editions use the round s. No j, no v, no q in Old English spelling.

lessons.title: Æ, Þ, Ð, Ƿ
lessons.content: Æ (ash) = the vowel in modern English 'cat.' Þ and ð (thorn and eth) = both the voiced and unvoiced th sounds; scribes used them interchangeably. Ƿ (wynn) = w. It looks like a p but is not.

lessons.title: Vowels and Diphthongs
lessons.content: Seven simple vowels: a, æ, e, i, o, u, y (the last pronounced like German ü). Four diphthongs: ea, eo, ie, io. Long vowels marked with macrons in modern editions but not in the manuscripts.

lessons.title: Consonants
lessons.content: C always hard (k). G can be guttural (as in modern German sagen) or a stop (as in modern English go) depending on position. Sc = sh. Cg = dge. H before a consonant or at word-end = German ch in 'ach.'

lessons.title: Stress
lessons.content: Almost always on the first syllable of the root. Prefixes (ge-, be-, for-) do not take stress.

lessons.title: First Words
lessons.content: Hwæt! — the opening word of Beowulf. Pronounced 'hwat,' not 'what.' Practice on ten common Old English words: hús (house), cyning (king), þegn (thane), sǽ (sea), mann (man), wíf (woman), bearn (child), word, déaþ (death), líf (life).

lessons.title: First Sentence
lessons.content: Ælfred kyning hateþ grétan Wærferþ biscep. — 'King Alfred commands Bishop Werferth to be greeted.' The opening of Alfred's preface to the Pastoral Care. Read it aloud ten times before moving on.

checkpoint.title: Stage 1 Checkpoint
checkpoint.format: Twenty letters and letter-combinations to identify by audio; ten words read aloud and recorded; five short sentences read aloud; ten modern English words transliterated into Old English spelling. Pass mark: 85%.

stages.name: The Sentence
stages.subtitle: The four cases, strong and weak nouns, strong verbs, the article; parsing before translating.
learning_outcomes: Decline any strong or weak noun in all four cases and both numbers.
Conjugate a strong verb (Classes I–VII) in the present and past indicative.
Recognize and parse the definite article se/seo/þæt in all its forms.
Translate simple sentences of the form Subject + Verb + Object with prepositional phrases and a genitive of possession.
Read fifty-word adapted passages from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Ælfric's prose.

lessons.title: The Four Cases
lessons.content: Nominative (subject), accusative (direct object), genitive (possession and partitive), dative (indirect object, instrument, accompaniment). Old English had a fifth case (instrumental) but it merged with the dative early.

lessons.title: The Definite Article
lessons.content: Se (masculine nominative), seo (feminine nominative), þæt (neuter nominative). Seventeen forms total. The article as the key to the gender and case of the noun.

lessons.title: Strong Nouns — Masculine a-Stems
lessons.content: Stán (stone), dæg (day), hlāf (loaf). Nominative stán, accusative stán, genitive stānes, dative stāne. Plural: stānas, stānas, stāna, stānum.

lessons.title: Strong Nouns — Neuter a-Stems
lessons.content: Scip (ship), word. Identical nominative and accusative in both numbers. Neuter plural nominative/accusative ends in -u or is unchanged.

lessons.title: Strong Nouns — Feminine ō-Stems
lessons.content: Giefu (gift), lufu (love), lār (teaching). Genitive singular -e, dative singular -e, nominative plural -a or -e.

lessons.title: Weak Nouns
lessons.content: Guma (man), sunne (sun), éage (eye). The -an declension. Simpler than the strong: most forms end in -an.

lessons.title: The Present Indicative of Strong Verbs
lessons.content: Rīdan (to ride) — Class I. Ic rīde, þū rītst, hē/hēo/hit rītt, wē/gē/hīe rīdaþ. The vowel alternation (ablaut) between present and past is the mark of a strong verb.

lessons.title: The Past Indicative of Strong Verbs
lessons.content: Ic rād, þū ride, hē rād, wē ridon. Seven ablaut classes. Each must be learned.

lessons.title: The Verb 'To Be'
lessons.content: Eom, eart, is, sind/sindon (present). Wæs, wǽre, wæs, wǽron (past). Irregular, essential, everywhere.

lessons.title: Adjectives — Strong and Weak
lessons.content: Gōd (good). Strong when used predicatively or without an article; weak after the article or a demonstrative. Se gōda cyning. Gōd cyning.

lessons.title: Prepositions and Case Government
lessons.content: On + dative (place where) or accusative (motion towards). Fram + dative (from). Mid + dative (with). Tō + dative (to).

lessons.title: Reading: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Year 449
lessons.content: Her Martianus and Valentinus onfengon rīce... — 'In this year Martianus and Valentinus received the kingdom.' First sustained reading. Fifty words, adapted, with full glosses.

lessons.title: Reading: Ælfric, on the Creation
lessons.content: On anginne gesceop God heofonan and eorþan. — 'In the beginning God created heaven and earth.' The opening of Genesis in Old English. Ælfric's clear, homiletic prose.

checkpoint.title: Stage 2 Checkpoint
checkpoint.format: Written. Decline ten nouns; conjugate five verbs; translate a seventy-five-word passage from the Chronicle or Ælfric; parse twenty inflected forms. Pass mark: 80%.

stages.name: The Reading
stages.subtitle: Caedmon's Hymn entire and the opening fifty lines of Beowulf. The capstone.
learning_outcomes: Read Caedmon's Hymn (nine lines, the oldest surviving Old English poem) in the original with notes and translate it into modern English.
Read the first fifty lines of Beowulf with notes and translate them.
Recognize and parse the poetic formulas (kennings, variation, alliterative meter) that distinguish Old English verse from prose.
Decline any i-stem or u-stem noun and conjugate weak verbs of both classes.
Translate any passage of thirty or fewer words from a glossed Old English prose or verse text at sight.

lessons.title: Weak Verbs — Class I
lessons.content: Dēman (to judge), hīeran (to hear). Present ic dēme, past ic dēmde. The dental suffix -d- marks the past tense.

lessons.title: Weak Verbs — Class II
lessons.content: Lufian (to love), macian (to make). The -ō- suffix in the first-person singular present.

lessons.title: Noun Declensions — i-Stems and u-Stems
lessons.content: Giest (guest), sunu (son), duru (door). Minor classes, common words.

lessons.title: Pronouns — Personal and Demonstrative
lessons.content: Ic, þū, hē, hēo, hit, wē, gē, hīe. The demonstrative þes, þēos, þis (this) versus se, seo, þæt (that / the).

lessons.title: The Subjunctive
lessons.content: Present ic rīde (same form as indicative in many verbs; context distinguishes), past ic ride. Used in wishes, commands, conditions, subordinate clauses after þæt or gif.

lessons.title: The Infinitive and the Participles
lessons.content: Infinitive: rīdan. Present participle: rīdende. Past participle: geriden. The ge- prefix marks completed action.

lessons.title: Old English Poetic Meter
lessons.content: Alliterative verse. Four stresses per line, divided by a caesura. The first three stresses alliterate; the fourth does not. No end-rhyme.

lessons.title: Kennings and Variation
lessons.content: Kenning: a compound metaphor (bānhūs = bone-house = body; hronrād = whale-road = sea). Variation: saying the same thing two different ways for emphasis (the king, the lord of men, the giver of rings).

lessons.title: Caedmon's Hymn — Lines 1–5
lessons.content: Nū sculon herigean heofonrīces Weard... — 'Now we must praise the Guardian of the heavenly kingdom.' First half of the hymn, with line-by-line grammatical commentary.

lessons.title: Caedmon's Hymn — Lines 6–9
lessons.content: ...Hē ǽrest sceōp eorðan bearnum / heofon tō hrōfe... — '...He first created for the children of earth / heaven as a roof.' The conclusion. Full translation and recitation.

lessons.title: Beowulf, Lines 1–11
lessons.content: Hwæt! Wē Gār-Dena in gēardagum... — 'Lo! We have heard of the Spear-Danes in days of yore.' The opening verse paragraph. Gloss and grammar on every word.

lessons.title: Beowulf, Lines 12–25
lessons.content: The lineage of Scyld Scefing. Introduction to the genealogical formulas (Scyld Scefing sceaþena þrēatum... — Scyld son of Sceaf, from the hosts of enemies).

lessons.title: Beowulf, Lines 26–50
lessons.content: The funeral of Scyld. The ship-burial. Poetic vocabulary (ȳþ-geblond = wave-tumult; sǽ-gēap = sea-curved). Full close reading.

lessons.title: Sight Reading Practice
lessons.content: Five short passages (twenty to thirty words each) from The Wanderer, The Seafarer, and Bede's Ecclesiastical History, with glosses but no grammatical notes. The student parses and translates at sight.

checkpoint.title: Stage 3 Capstone Examination
checkpoint.format: Written, three hours. Translate Caedmon's Hymn entire from memory or from the text (student's choice). Translate Beowulf lines 1–50 with notes. Translate one thirty-word sight passage from a glossed Old English prose text. Parse fifteen inflected forms. Pass mark: 70%. Honors: 85%.

certification.credential_name: The Kalopaideia Diploma in Reading Old English
certification.credential_subtitle: An attestation that the bearer has completed the three-stage course and passed the capstone examination.
certification.what_it_is: A privately-issued certificate of completion. Not an academic degree. Not a teaching license. It says: this person sat down with the language of Beowulf and Bede and earned an honest reading of it.
certification.what_is_recorded: Student's chosen public name; the language; the date of the capstone examination; the result (Pass or Pass with Honors); the SHA-256 hash of the student's signed examination scripts.
certification.what_is_not_recorded: The actual examination answers; the student's email or other identifiers; anything that could identify the student against their will. The certificate is pseudonymous if the student wishes.
certification.issuance: On-chain on Base as an ERC-721 soulbound (non-transferable) token. One certificate per student per language. The contract is owned by Kalopaideia and the minting key is held by the proprietor. The token URI points to a permanent, IPFS-pinned JSON document signed by Kalopaideia's issuing key.
certification.verification: Any third party can verify a certificate at kalopaideia.com/verify/<token-id> by entering the token ID and the certificate hash. The page will display the issuance date, the language, and the result.
certification.cost: Included in the Akousma subscription. The on-chain gas fee at issuance is paid by Kalopaideia. The student pays nothing extra.
certification.renewability: None. A diploma is not a driver's license. Once earned, it stands.
